title: Intent-to-Action Tooling Demo - Sierra Systems
summary: Overview/demo of Redwood JSON mode (schemas + guardrails), tool/function calling, Console sandbox and Optimize recommendations. Discussed security/VPC, KMS, pilot scope and next steps.
transcript:
Meeting: Intent-to-Action Tooling Demo - Sierra Systems
Date: 2026-12-11 15:00 PST
Duration: 52 min
Attendees: Jordan Liu, Priya Menon (Redwood); Martin Kline, Aisha Rahman, Derek Cole, Leah Ortiz (Sierra)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/docs/json-mode , https://redwood.ai/console/sandbox , https://redwood.ai/security/soc2

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, today we're going to run through a focused demo on intent-to-action tooling — basically how you can go from user intent all the way to safe tool invocations using Redwood's JSON mode. Priya and I will tag team. can you hear us okay?

[00:12] Martin: yes, loud and clear. excited to see how you handle schema enforcement — we've had weird outputs from models in the past.

[01:12] Priya: great. quick agenda — 1) show JSON mode and schema editor in the Console 2) tool calling patterns (sync/async) 3) runtime guardrails & fallback orchestration 4) Optimize recommendations for cost/latency. we'll sprinkle in notes about private deployment options and security.

[05:03] Priya: starting in the Console — here's the sandbox. you can paste a JSON schema or pick from templates. watch as I define a simple action schema for "create_support_ticket": fields are severity, summary, user_id, attachments_url. I'm going to intentionally mark severity as enum so the model must pick one of [low, medium, high].

[05:40] Aisha: quick q — if the model hallucinated an extra field, does the runtime strip it or fail?

[05:50] Priya: good question. by default JSON mode will validate against the schema. you can choose a strict reject policy, which returns a structured error, or set a best-effort mode that emits corrections via the "diagnostics" object. we recommend strict for actionable tool calls.

[08:47] Jordan: switching to tool calling — you can register connectors as typed functions in the Console. here, I demo wiring the create_support_ticket action to a webhook that posts to your internal ticketing API (we'll also show a mocked call). note: auth secrets are behind KMS and never emitted to the model.

[12:10] Derek: what about partial failures? if the ticket create fails, can you fall back to a synchronous human review route?

[12:30] Priya: absolutely. the rollout includes policies: if external call fails or returns 5xx, runtime can do a canary retry to a secondary endpoint, or mark the action for human review and call an escalator webhook. we'll demo the fallback orchestration in a minute.

[15:25] Jordan: now showing the API flow — a snippet: POST /v1/generate with mode: "json", schema: <schema_id>, functions: [create_support_ticket]. the model returns a typed payload ready to invoke. note the response includes a kv_cache key for prefix cache hits and a request_id for tracing. (transcript note: 'KV cash' heard in places, should be 'KV cache')

[19:01] Leah: security — we need SSO, audit logs, encryption at rest, and key management. how do you integrate with our corporate KMS?

[19:18] Jordan: we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM providers. Customer-managed keys are supported and key rotation is logged. console shows the audit trail and per-request metadata; we also ship syslog/forwarding for SIEM. we are SOC 2 certified — see link I shared.

[23:40] Priya: demoing a live failure to show guardrails — I altered the mock so the webhook returns 500. watch: runtime picks that up, marks the action failed, triggers fallback policy (retry->secondary->escalate). the transcript shows the model suggesting a human escalate with reasons.

[27:10] Martin: curious about latency implications. we care about 95th pct under 300ms for short actions. how does JSON validation and the extra orchestration affect P95?

[27:35] Priya: validation is nanoseconds compared to inference; the main latency is model generation and external call. Optimize will recommend batching profiles and a small quantized model for high QPS. for webhook calls we recommend async invites so you don't block user-facing flows; returning an acceptance token can keep UI latency low.

[31:55] Jordan: switching to Optimize — here's an example workload where we profiled support routing: average token length 150, lots of repeated prefixes. Optimize suggested caching the first 80 tokens (prefix K/V cache) and enabling continuous batching with a max batch size of 8 on dedicated instances. projected cost down by ~38% and P95 down ~22% in our sim.

[36:20] Aisha: about models — can we run our in-house fine-tuned model or do we have to use models in Redwood catalog?

[36:40] Priya: both. the platform supports customer model artifacts in Private deployments and can also host your model in Dedicated if you want predictable SLA. you'll need to upload a model tar + config; we do a quick compatibility check to suggest kernels and quantization paths.

[41:05] Derek: any restrictions on tool payload size? some of our tickets include long transcripts.

[41:25] Jordan: payload size depends on route and runtime memory; we recommend offloading bulky blobs to a storage service and passing an attachments_url. the runtime will stream the model output and not materialize huge JSON in memory unless you opt-in.

[46:00] Priya: quick note on safety & guardrails — we showed enum enforcement, reject policies, and fallback orchestration. additionally you can block certain tool calls with RBAC hooks and a deny list at the route level. the Console policy editor attaches to rollouts so you can test in sandbox.

[50:10] Jordan: recap — key takeaway: JSON mode gives you typed outputs that are safe to call as functions; Console makes schema authoring and sandboxing easy; Optimize reduces cost/latency with concrete recommendations; and Private/VPC/KMS options satisfy common enterprise controls.

[51:30] Martin: looks good. next steps — we'd like a pilot: 6 week POC, scope around support-ticket automation and triage. Leah will lead security review. can you share pricing and a SOC2 pack?

[51:45] Jordan: yes — we'll send a pilot proposal, pricing sheet, and SOC2 + architecture diagram. action items below. thanks everyone.

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-heard terms (e.g., 'KV cash', 'SAM EL' for SAML) and generic speaker tags in a couple places.
next_steps: Send 6-week pilot proposal and statement of work
Share SOC2 pack and architecture diagram
Schedule security deep-dive with Leah and infra team
Provide pricing sheet for Dedicated pilot
